source.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing

page_placements.theme: Language-model neurons often carry several behaviours or lack a clean label

record.file_problem: The text contains the post's abstract and contribution summary, plus comments, but not the full paper or its detailed methods and results.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse probing rather than the claim's neuron-pole audit. Its reported findings about superposition, seemingly dedicated neurons, and scaling bear conceptually on neuron interpretability and its distribution.
record.gate_note: The excerpt reports qualitative findings about sparse representations and scaling, but no neuron-pole percentages, two-job category, or unexplained-neuron share. It does not report held-out tests of natural-language explanations or activation-prediction scores. The comment citing the OpenAI neuron-explanation work is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study trains k-sparse probes from input features to neurons. It does not audit a population of neurons for how many have one main job, two related jobs or none. It reports no neuron-share percentages, no explanation-vs-activation tests and no simulation scores. Its findings bear on the related question of how features map onto neurons and where superposition occurs, but they do not measure any version's quantity, so they go under fits_no_version. The excerpt is only the abstract and contribution summary.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find a great deal of interpretable structure in LLM neurons and present sparse probing as effective but needing careful follow-up. Early layers use superposition of polysemantic neurons, and middle layers have seemingly monosemantic neurons for contextual features, though conclusive monosemanticity claims are out of reach. Sparsity increases with scale on average, with varied per-feature dynamics.
record.recipe_differences: Uses k-sparse linear probes to identify neurons relevant to input features, rather than generating explanations of neuron poles and testing those explanations on activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported findings differ by layer and feature; the excerpt also says scaling dynamics differ across features.

fits_no_version.finding: Many early-layer neurons are polysemantic. Each activates for many unrelated n-grams, and features are represented as sparse combinations of such neurons. The authors infer the first 25% of MLP layers use substantially more superposition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small-to-mid language models (Pythia 70M–6.9B), early-layer neurons are predominantly polysemantic and represent features in superposition, contrary to a uniform 'one main job' picture across layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher-level contextual features (e.g., is_python_code) seem to have dedicated neurons, mostly in middle layers. Average sparsity rises with scale, with mixed per-feature dynamics (emergence, splitting, unchanged).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron monosemanticity for probed features varies by layer depth and grows on average with model scale.

record.problems: The supplied excerpt omits detailed methods, per-model results, and numeric measurements of monosemanticity or pole shares. The reported monosemanticity finding is explicitly tentative.
record.rows_left_out: No study results stated in the excerpt were omitted. The commenter’s reference to the separate OpenAI neuron-explanation work is not a result of this study.

untested.parts: All of it: no neuron-pole audit and no shares, and Qwen3-32B is not studied.
All of it: no cross-model neuron shares, no MoE models, and nothing beyond 6.9B parameters.
No comparison of tools or architectures for interpretable-neuron share.
No held-out test of explanations against activations.

record.verdict_notes: Only the LessWrong summary was available, not the full paper. The reader's 'tests'/T2 with V1/V2 limits_scope labels is overturned: the study reports no neuron-share measure, so its results cannot qualify the versions' quantities. The comment linking OpenAI's neuron-explanation work (an original source) is not a result of this study. The subject models are presumably Pythia, but the excerpt does not name them.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure the percentages of poles with one job, two related jobs, or no known job, and does not test the Qwen3-32B audit.
Does not measure the claimed shares across models; the excerpt reports models only up to 6.9 billion parameters, not trillions, and does not specify dense versus mixture-of-experts coverage.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or pose-feature analysis is reported.
Does not test the essay's InceptionV1-sized estimates or causally compare architectures, regularization, or tools.
No attribution-graph reconstruction test is reported.
No test of explanations against where neurons activate, using examples not used to write the explanation, is reported.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text is reported.

rows.subject: 7 language models (not individually named in the excerpt)
rows.operation_detail: Used sparse linear probes to study how features are represented in neuron activations.

conditions.value: early layers; first 25% of fully connected layers

rows.value: Many early-layer neurons represent features in superposition; the first 25% of fully connected layers employ substantially more superposition than the rest.
rows.note: The first-25% comparison is attributed to weight statistics and insights from toy models. This is not a measurement of the share of neuron poles with one job.
rows.check: Measures feature-to-neuron sparsity and superposition in early layers, not the share of neurons with one main job. The 'first 25%' conclusion rests on weight statistics and toy-model insight, not a direct count. It cannot be read as a V1 state, and the subject is not Qwen3-32B.

rows.subject: 7 language models (not individually named in the excerpt)
rows.operation_detail: Probed internal activations for high-level contextual and linguistic features.
rows.measure: Whether features appear to be encoded by dedicated neurons
rows.value: Such features are seemingly encoded by monosemantic neurons, predominantly in middle layers; the authors say conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
rows.note: The finding is tentative and limited to the probed features; it does not establish an overall share of monosemantic neuron poles.
rows.check: Reports seemingly dedicated neurons for probed contextual features in middle layers. It gives no share of neurons, and the authors say monosemanticity conclusions are out of reach. Not a V1 measure.

rows.subject: 7 language models (not individually named in the excerpt)
rows.operation_detail: Compared representation sparsity across models of different sizes.

conditions.value: models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters

rows.measure: Representation sparsity and its scaling dynamics
rows.value: Representation sparsity increases on average with model size, but dynamics differ by feature: some dedicated neurons emerge, some features split into finer-grained features, and many remain unchanged or appear somewhat randomly.
rows.note: The excerpt gives an aggregate finding across the models, not separate per-model values or the claimed shares of one-job, two-job, and unexplained poles.
rows.check: Measures average representation sparsity versus scale (70M–6.9B), not shares of one-job, two-job or unexplained neurons across models. Not a V2 measure.

relation.reason: The study discusses neuron polysemanticity, superposition and seemingly monosemantic middle-layer neurons. It does not test the claim's versions.

tranche.reason: Sparse probing from input features to neurons does not audit what share of neurons have one main job. It reports no shares, explanation-vs-activation tests or simulation scores, so it tests no version. The polysemanticity finding is a related construct, recorded correctly under fits-no-version. The reader's earlier T2 call is not supported.

source_check.notes: The text is the LessWrong post: abstract, contributions and comments only, not the body of arXiv 2305.01610. It names no model family; Pythia fits the stated 7 models, 70M to 6.9B. The 'first 25%' conclusion rests on weight statistics and toy-model insight, not a direct measurement. No verdicts are listed, which is correct.

statements.problem: No substantive error. The numbers (70M to 6.9B, first 25%) and both claims match the Contributions text. 'Infer' fits 'based on weight statistics and insights from toy models, we conclude'. 'MLP layers' is the same as 'fully connected layers'. This post does not name the model family (it says 7 models, 70M to 6.9B). Nothing in the text contradicts Pythia, and that suite covers the stated range.
